catalog_locator: Thesis p. 23, sec. 1.2.3.3 'Consonant-vowel effects, phonotactics and prosody', last paragraph; also p. 6. Speech Prosody 2012 paper p. 91, sec. 2.1 'Corpus'. SP 2014 paper sec. 2 'Methods'; SP 2016 paper sec. 2 'Methods'.
catalog_quote: [Graetzer 2012 thesis, p. 23] With regard to lexical prosody, an early analysis by Lowe (1975) suggests that primary stress is on the first syllable of the word and secondary stress is on alternate syllables thereafter with the exception of the final syllable, e.g., <burgu> /'buɹgu/ ‘flower’ (Butcher, forthcoming b). Long vowels occur only in the word-initial syllable, e.g., <bäpa> /bɐ:pɐ/ ‘father’ but not *<bapä> (Lowe, 1975). See also §2.4.3. [p. 6] The majority of Australian languages, including Burarra and Gupapuyngu, show predominantly word-initial stress (Goedemans, 2010). [Graetzer, Hajek & Fletcher 2012, p. 91] On the basis of the intonational analysis (which assumed that the vowel carrying a sharp F0 rise to a peak somewhere in or around the syllable rhyme was accentually prominent), vowels were identified as being prominent or not prominent. In the CV1.CV2 words, such as <gapu> /gapu/, V1 is prosodically prominent (associated with regular non-final lexical stress) and V2 is both prosodically weak and word-final. [Graetzer, Fletcher & Hajek 2014, sec. 2] Main stress was word-initial in these data. Words were associated with post-lexical (or phrasal) prosodic prominence ... [Graetzer, Fletcher & Hajek 2016, sec. 2] In this data set, the main stress was word-initial. Words were uttered in isolation, and hence, as mentioned, were associated with phrasal prosodic prominence.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (317-page PDF, text; extracted text). p. 44 = printed p. 23, sec. 1.2.3.3 'Consonant-vowel effects, phonotactics and prosody'. The quoted passage is there verbatim (line breaks aside): 'With regard to lexical prosody, an early analysis by Lowe (1975) suggests that primary stress is on the first syllable of the word and secondary stress is on alternate syllables thereafter with the exception of the final syllable, e.g., <burgu> /'buɹgu/ 'flower' (Butcher, forthcoming b). Long vowels occur only in the word-initial syllable, e.g., <bäpa> /bɐ:pɐ/ 'father' but not *<bapä> (Lowe, 1975). See also §2.4.3.' Also confirmed p. 6 (the text): 'The majority of Australian languages, including Burar…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of every word; secondary stresses fall on alternate syllables after it (third, fifth..), but never on the final syllable. Long vowels are confined to the stressed initial syllable. Graetzer and colleagues' own acoustic corpus (three female speakers, citation-form CVCV words, F0-peak-based prominence labelling) confirms the initial syllable as the prominent one ('main stress was word-initial in these data', 2014 and 2016 papers).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Per Lowe 1975 as reported by Graetzer 2012 p. 23: on alternate syllables after the initial one, excluding the final syllable (i.e. left-to-right trochaic alternation with final-syllable extrametricality). Not tested instrumentally (corpus is disyllabic).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for Gupapuyngu. For the sibling Dhuwal varieties, Morphy 1983 (Djapu, p. 25) and Amery 1985 (Yirrkala Yolngu Matha, p. 36) say stress is 'almost always' initial with a handful of exceptions, chiefly words whose second syllable begins with /d/ (Morphy, citing Schebeck).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical stress). The instrumental corpus consists of isolated citation-form CV1.CV2 words, so word stress and phrasal (nuclear) accent coincide on the initial syllable; the 2014/2016 papers say this explicitly. The full alternating rule is Graetzer's report of Lowe's 1975 pedagogical pronunciation booklet, not an independent analysis; the first-hand element is the acoustic identification of the initial syllable as the stressed one.
new_statements.identity_note: Gupapuyngu (Gupapuyŋu, Gobabingo) is the western, Yirritja-moiety Dhuwala variety of Dhuwal-Dhuwala (Yolngu), spoken at Milingimbi, Ramingining, Gapuwiyak and Galiwin'ku. Graetzer's corpus: three adult female Gupapuyngu speakers (AM, BT, EG, aged 40-49) recorded by Andrew Butcher 1988-1991, community not stated. Lowe's 1975 booklet is Galiwin'ku/Milingimbi Gupapuyngu. The Djapu (Morphy 1983) and Yirrkala (Amery 1985) statements held by the project under guma1253 describe sibling Dhuwal varieties (Dhuwal = dhuw1249), not Gupapuyngu itself.

new_statements.quote: [p. 66, Fig. 1 legend:] Main stress is (predominantly) initial [white] / Main stress is (predominantly) penultimate [dark grey] / Unclear; key: Gupapuyngu 7 [no. 7 is in the white area]. [p. 72:] The most striking example is Nunggubuyu (Hore 1981), a language spoken on the east coast, close to the strictly left oriented Yolngu languages. [p. 77:] First of all, it must be noted that the white area in the northeast corner of Arnhem Land in figure 1 is probably not indicative of "a remnant pocket" of initial stress languages that are gradually being overtaken by the penultimate stress rule. [...] Their languages (no's 7, 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13 in figure 1) are related to Western Desert, rather than to any non-Pama-Nyungan language.

Goedemans & E. van Zanten (eds.), A Survey of Word Accentual Patterns in the Languages of the World, 55-85. Berlin/New York: De Gruyter Mouton. (Miriwung = language no. 51 on the stress map)

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Re-opened the copy consulted (896 pp., text). All three quoted passages are present verbatim: p. 80 = book p. 66 (Figure 1 legend 'Main stress is (predominantly) initial' / '(predominantly) penultimate' / 'Unclear'; key 'Gupapuyngu 7'; footnote 6 'scores of exceptions with, sometimes even regularised, antepenultimate or initial stress'); p. 86 = book p. 72 ('The most striking example is Nunggubuyu (Hore 1981), a language spoken on the east coast, close to the strictly left oriented Yolngu languages.'); p. 91 = book p. 77 ('the white area in the northeast corner of Arnhem Land in figure 1 is probably not indicative of "a remnant pocket" of initial stress languages.. Their languages (no's 7,…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (fixed, initial: initial stress) and as the existing Graetzer 2012 / Lowe 1975 statement (primary stress on the first syllable). Adds no detail on secondary stress or exceptions for Gupapuyngu itself, so it confirms rather than refines. Note the citation string in the target list says 'Miriwung = language no. 51 on the stress map'; for this item the relevant map number is Gupapuyngu = 7 (Miriwung is a different language, no. 51, in the 'unclear' area).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Goedemans classifies Gupapuyngu (language no. 7 on his Arnhem Land stress map) among the 'strictly left oriented' Yolngu languages, i.e. main stress (predominantly) on the initial syllable. The classification is map-level only: no Gupapuyngu examples or per-language description are given; the map is 'compiled with data from, among others, Wurm and Hattori (1981) and Dixon (1980)' and the caption says 'details ignored'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing specific to Gupapuyngu. The chapter's general 'basic Australian pattern' (Mantjiltjara type, p. 57-58) has initial main stress with secondary stress on alternate syllables left-to-right and no stress on a leftover final syllable, but Goedemans does not say which Yolngu languages share the secondary-stress rule. The volume's StressTyp appendix (Part II, p. 672) has no Gupapuyngu entry; its only Yolngu entry is Gaalpu (dialect of Dhangu) [I]: 'Primary stress on the first syllable. Secondary stress on the penult or antepenult of words longer than three syllables' (Wood 1978).
new_statements.exceptions: Only the blanket caveat in footnote 6 (p. 66): 'We also abstract away from competing patterns. Most of the languages mentioned here have scores of exceptions with, sometimes even regularised, antepenultimate or initial stress.' Nothing Gupapuyngu-specific.
new_statements.identity_note: Goedemans treats Gupapuyngu as one of six Yolngu languages on his map (nos. 7 Gupapuyngu, 9 Djinang, 10 Djinba, 11 Dhuwal, 12 Djapu, 13 Ritharngu), all in the initial-stress (white) area; he does not name a dialect or a source specific to Gupapuyngu. The same volume's StressTyp data section describes only Gaalpu (a Dhangu dialect, Yolngu) from Wood 1978, not Gupapuyngu.
